extracted.intended_audience: NeurIPS program committee members, area chairs, reviewers, and ML researchers interested in peer review/process evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines, scoring rubrics, and an analysis workflow for reviewing NeurIPS conference submissions (quality/impact/confidence scores, qualitative criteria, reviewer calibration, duplicate-paper experiment and Monte Carlo acceptance probability estimation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Score (1–10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers give a score of between 1 and 10 for each paper. The program committee will interpret the numerical score in the following way:
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
10: Top 5% of accepted NIPS papers, a seminal paper for the ages. I will consider not reviewing for NIPS again if this is rejected.
9: Top 15% of accepted NIPS papers, an excellent paper, a strong accept. I will fight for acceptance.
8: Top 50% of accepted NIPS papers, a very good paper, a clear accept. I vote and argue for acceptance.
7: Good paper, accept. I vote for acceptance, although would not be upset if it were rejected.
6: Marginally above the acceptance threshold. I tend to vote for accepting it, but leaving it out of the program would be no great loss.
5: Marginally below the acceptance threshold. I tend to vote for rejecting it, but having it in the program would not be that bad.
4: An OK paper, but not good enough. A rejection. I vote for rejecting it, although would not be upset if it were accepted.
3: A clear rejection. I vote and argue for rejection.
2: A strong rejection. I’m surprised it was submitted to this conference. I will fight for rejection.
1: Trivial or wrong or known. I’m surprised anybody wrote such a paper. I will consider not reviewing for NIPS again if this is accepted.
Additional guidance: "Reviewers should NOT assume that they have received an unbiased sample of papers, nor should they adjust their scores to achieve an artificial balance of high and low scores. Scores should reflect absolute judgments of the contributions made by each paper."

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact Score (binary / 1–2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independently of the Quality Score above, this is your opportunity to identify papers that are very different, original, or otherwise potentially impactful for the NIPS community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Two choices:
2: This work is different enough from typical submissions to potentially have a major impact on a subset of the NIPS community.
1: This work is incremental and unlikely to have much impact even though it may be technically correct and well executed.
Guidance: Impact and quality may point in opposite directions (e.g., technically strong but unlikely to generate follow-up research, or flawed but likely to open new directions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence Score (1–5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers also give a confidence score between 1 and 5 for each paper. The program committee will interpret the numerical score as follows:
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature.
4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct. It is unlikely but conceivable that the reviewer did not understand certain parts of the paper, or that the reviewer was unfamiliar with a piece of relevant literature.
3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct. It is possible that the reviewer did not understand certain parts of the paper, or that the reviewer was unfamiliar with a piece of relevant literature. Mathematics and other details were not carefully checked.
2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper.
1: The reviewer’s evaluation is an educated guess. Either the paper is not in the reviewer’s area, or it was extremely difficult to understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative Evaluation — Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper technically sound? Are claims well-supported by theoretical analysis or experimental results? Is this a complete piece of work, or merely a position paper? Are the authors careful (and honest) about evaluating both the strengths and weaknesses of the work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should comment on this criterion where possible; consider reproducibility and whether the evidence supports claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative Evaluation — Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper clearly written? Is it well-organized? Does it adequately inform the reader?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A superbly written paper provides enough information for the expert reader to reproduce its results. If not clear, reviewers should suggest improvements to the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative Evaluation — Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the problems or approaches new? Is this a novel combination of familiar techniques? Is it clear how this work differs from previous contributions? Is related work adequately referenced?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are recommended to check recent NIPS proceedings to ensure the paper is significantly different from previous proceedings; abstracts and links to previous NIPS papers are available. Comment on novelty and relation to prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative Evaluation — Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results important? Are other people (practitioners or researchers) likely to use these ideas or build on them? Does the paper address a difficult problem in a better way than previous research?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the paper advances the state of the art in a demonstrable way, or provides unique data or conclusions that others will build on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer workload limits
rubrics_metrics.description: To keep quality of reviews high, reviewer load was limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We didn’t assign any reviewer more than 5 papers; most reviewers received 4 papers. Keep load low to maintain review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria used to recruit reviewers/area chairs for the program committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek individuals with at least two previously-published papers from NeurIPS and other leading ML venues such as ICML, AISTATS, COLT, UAI, etc.; use DBLP to verify publication track record. Recruit area chairs first and use them to nominate reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate-paper experiment procedure (10% duplication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximately 10% of submissions were randomly selected to be reviewed twice, by independent committees, to measure review consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 170 papers were selected from 1678 submissions. Program committee was split into two; reviewers were placed randomly on one side or the other. For Program Chairs some manual selection ensured expert coverage on both sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer calibration model (bias correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model reviewer scores as y_{i,j} = f_i + b_j + ε_{i,j} where f_i is objective paper quality, b_j is reviewer offset, ε is reviewer-specific noise; assume normal priors and estimate parameters to correct biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumptions: ε_{i,j} ~ N(0,σ^2), f_i ~ N(μ,α_f), b_j ~ N(0,α_b). Reparameterize to α_f with normalized ratios α_b/α_f and σ^2/α_f; fit via maximum likelihood (or GPy) to recover α_f and other parameters, then compute calibrated paper scores and reviewer offsets. Use these calibrated scores for downstream Monte Carlo acceptance simulations and bias reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score independence / absolute judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction to reviewers about how to use the scoring scale relative to the sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Reviewers should NOT assume that they have received an unbiased sample of papers, nor should they adjust their scores to achieve an artificial balance of high and low scores. Scores should reflect absolute judgments of the contributions made by each paper."

rubrics_metrics.name: Monte Carlo acceptance probability estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the posterior distribution of bias-adjusted (calibrated) scores to sample conference outcomes and estimate per-paper probability of acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute calibrated mean s and covariance covs, sample jointly from a multivariate normal (e.g., 1000 samples), rank papers in each sample and accept the top N (number_accepts set to conference target, e.g., 420). The proportion of samples where a paper is accepted gives its AcceptProbability. Use this to identify 'grey area' papers for discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grey-area boundaries for discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of the probability interval for papers that will be debated heavily during teleconferences between program chairs and area chairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define lower and upper bounds (example: lower = 0.1, upper = 0.9). Papers with AcceptProbability between these bounds are in the 'grey area' and require more debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer bias adjustment reporting and export
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute posterior mean and standard deviation for reviewer offsets and optionally export bias corrections for use in the review management system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute b = K_b * alpha and covb = α_f*(K_b - K_b K^{-1} K_b). Aggregate per-reviewer mean adjustments and std, produce histograms and export (example: bias_export prepared for CMT). Use these for sanity checks and to inform calibration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment/process summary metrics (inconsistency, accept precision, reject precision, agreed accept rate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics to summarize agreement/inconsistency between independent committees in the duplicate-paper experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Inconsistency: proportion of decisions that were not the same across the two committees (example 43/166 = 0.259).
Accept precision: probability an accepted paper would be rejected in an independent rerun — computed for committee i as accepted-and-rejected counts (example averaging committees to get ~0.495).
Reject precision: probability a rejected paper would be rejected again (example ~0.825 average).
Agreed accept rate: ratio of consistent accepts to consistent rejects (example 22/101 = 0.218). These formulas and interpretations are given in the text.
